content: Urgent care refers to the provision of outpatient medical services in facilities specifically designed to handle unscheduled, walk-in patients who require immediate attention but do not have conditions severe enough to necessitate a visit to a hospital emergency department. These centers are primarily utilized for treating injuries or illnesses that need prompt care but are not life-threatening. Unlike hospital emergency rooms, urgent care centers are not typically open 24/7. The first urgent care centers were established in the 1970s, and since then, the sector has grown significantly, with approximately 17,000 centers now in operation. Many of these facilities were initiated by entrepreneurial physicians responding to the public's demand for convenient access to unscheduled medical care. Others have been developed by hospital systems aiming to attract more patients. The rapid expansion of urgent care centers has been driven by the cost savings they offer compared to hospital emergency departments. Managed care organizations (MCOs) often encourage their members to use urgent care services as a cost-effective alternative. Urgent care centers are distinct from other ambulatory healthcare facilities. Emergency departments, for example, are located within hospitals and are equipped to handle true medical emergencies, such as myocardial infarctions (heart attacks), severe motor vehicle accidents, suicide attempts, and other life-threatening conditions. These departments are staffed by physicians with specialized training or board certification in emergency medicine and have immediate access to major surgical and critical care units. Most U.S. states require hospitals to have an emergency department on-site, though some states permit freestanding emergency departments, which are often considered high-acuity urgent care centers rather than true emergency departments. Primary care offices with extended hours may offer evening and weekend services, but unless they accept walk-in patients during all operating hours, provide on-site X-ray facilities, and treat simple fractures and lacerations, they are not classified as urgent care centers. Similarly, walk-in primary care offices do not qualify as urgent care facilities unless they provide expanded services and significant after-hours care. Retail-based medical offices, which began appearing in 2004, offer limited medical services in retail stores with on-site pharmacies. These clinics are typically staffed by nurse practitioners or physician assistants, and their prices are often publicly displayed. While some experts view these clinics as a future trend in consumer-driven healthcare, they are not considered true urgent care centers due to their limited scope of care, lack of on-site physicians, and absence of X-ray facilities. Concerns about potential conflicts of interest and over-prescription of medications in these settings remain unresolved. The Urgent Care Association of America (UCAOA) plays a significant role in the industry, hosting annual conventions and conferences. Other organizations, such as the American Academy of Urgent Care Medicine (AAUCM) and the National Association for Ambulatory Urgent Care (NAFAC), also hold joint annual conventions. Many industry leaders anticipate the formal recognition of urgent care as a medical specialty, complete with fellowship and residency programs to train physicians in the unique patient presentations and care requirements of urgent care centers. In recent years, the American Medical Association approved the UCM (Urgent Care Medicine) code, allowing physicians to self-designate as specialists in urgent care medicine. Services provided in urgent care centers can be identified using the place of service code POS-20 on CMS-1500 forms submitted to third-party payers. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) have designated specific codes for urgent care centers, such as S9083 (global fee for urgent care centers) and S9088 (services rendered in an urgent care center). Due to the complexity of coding for urgent care services, the UCAOA offers advanced coding workshops during its annual fall conference. In 2006, the UCAOA sponsored the first fellowship training program in urgent care medicine, a collaboration between the Department of Family Medicine at University Hospitals of Cleveland/Case School of Medicine, the UCAOA, and University Primary and Specialty Care Practices, Inc. in Cleveland, Ohio. This program, partially funded by a $30,000 unrestricted grant from the UCAOA, provides physicians with training in various disciplines essential for urgent care practice, including adult and pediatric emergencies, wound and injury management, occupational medicine, urgent care procedures, and the business aspects of running an urgent care center. A second fellowship program was launched in 2007 at the University of Illinois. These one-year fellowships are open to graduates of accredited Family Medicine and Med/Peds residency programs. The official publication of the UCAOA is the Journal of Urgent Care Medicine (JUCM), a monthly journal tailored for professionals in the urgent care industry. The American Academy of Urgent Care Medicine also publishes a monthly journal, Urgent Care, which is available for free to licensed physicians who subscribe. Point-of-care medication dispensing allows urgent care practitioners to ensure that patients receive their prescriptions before leaving the clinic. To offer this service, urgent care centers must partner with point-of-care dispensing corporations. The emergence of specialized industries supporting urgent care, such as practice management software and group purchasing organizations (GPOs), highlights the sector's growing importance. GPOs enable urgent care centers to collectively negotiate pricing, a benefit previously limited to hospitals. Malpractice insurance tailored to the urgent care industry has also gained attention. Many insurers fail to recognize the reduced malpractice risk associated with urgent care centers. However, some insurers offer policies with features such as no charge for tail coverage (coverage for claims arising after policy termination), rapid approval of new providers, no additional premiums for adding providers, per-visit full-time equivalent (FTE) rating, and lower premiums.
